intro: A fertilizer bag says 3 pounds per 1,000 square feet. A taxi meter climbs $2 every mile. A bake sale has one table, one budget and one goal. Each of these is a rule that can be written with letters and solved. This unit is Algebra I: the tools for writing a situation as an equation, an inequality or a function, solving it with steps you can justify, and checking that the number you get makes sense in the real world.

You will start with single equations and inequalities, treating each as a statement that must stay true while you undo operations on both sides. Then you will meet functions, rules with a name, an input and exactly one output, and learn to read f(3) as a question with an answer. Linear functions get special attention, because a constant rate of change describes fares, pay, savings and draining tanks. Finally you will solve two conditions at once with systems, and find the best plan inside a region of limits.

By the end you will be able to solve multi-step equations and inequalities with reasons, rearrange any formula, build a linear model from a table or a story and use it to predict, and solve a system by graphing, substitution or elimination. Most of all, you will have the habit of checking: substitute the answer back, compare it to an estimate, and read it back into the story.
bigQuestion: How do letters, equations and graphs let us turn a real situation into a question we can answer with certainty?

story.title: The Formula on the Back of the Fertilizer Bag
story.kicker: A community garden, a 20-pound bag, and one line of small print that turns out to be algebra.
paragraphs: Jasmine volunteers on Saturdays at a community garden on the South Side of Chicago. In April the garden coordinator hands her a 20-pound bag of fertilizer and points at the raised beds. "Spread the right amount," she says, "too little does nothing and too much burns the roots." Jasmine flips the bag over. On the back, in small print, is one sentence: apply 3 pounds for every 1,000 square feet.

That sentence is a formula in disguise. Jasmine paces off the main bed: 40 feet by 60 feet. She multiplies to get the area, 40 × 60 = 2,400 square feet. Then she reasons: 2,400 is 2.4 groups of 1,000, so she needs 2.4 × 3 = 7.2 pounds. She writes the rule with letters so she never has to think it through again: pounds = 0.003 × area, because 3 ÷ 1,000 = 0.003. Check: 0.003 × 2,400 = 7.2. It matches.

Now the coordinator asks the question backwards. "We have 20 pounds. How much ground can one bag cover?" This time the pounds are known and the area is the mystery. Jasmine writes 20 = 0.003 × A and asks herself what undoes multiplying by 0.003. Dividing by 0.003 does. So A = 20 ÷ 0.003, which is about 6,667 square feet. One bag covers the main bed almost three times over.

By the end of the morning Jasmine has used the same formula four different ways: forward, backward, for a bed shaped like an L, and to decide whether one bag is enough for the whole season. Every time, she does one thing: she treats the equation as a sentence that must stay true, and she does the same thing to both sides. That single habit is what this chapter is about.
story.think: The bag says 3 pounds per 1,000 square feet. Jasmine's friend says a 30-by-30-foot bed needs 9 pounds. Is he right? Explain how you would check without a calculator.

lessons.title: True, False or Open
lessons.mainIdea: An equation is a statement that can be true or false, and a solution is a value that makes it true.
reading: Look at three sentences: 3 + 4 = 7, 3 + 4 = 8, and x + 4 = 7. The first is true. The second is false. The third is neither, because it has a blank in it. A sentence with a variable is called an *open sentence*: it becomes true or false only after you fill in a number. Fill in 3 and you get 3 + 4 = 7, true. Fill in 5 and you get 5 + 4 = 7, false. So an *equation* is not a command to "do something." It is a claim that two sides are equal, and your job is to find out when that claim holds.

A number that makes the equation true is a *solution*. To test a number, you *substitute* it for the variable and simplify both sides. Is 5 a solution of 2x − 3 = 7? Substitute: 2(5) − 3 = 10 − 3 = 7. The left side is 7, the right side is 7, so yes. Is 4 a solution? 2(4) − 3 = 8 − 3 = 5, and 5 is not 7, so no. This testing step is the most important habit in algebra, because it works no matter how you found the number.

Students sometimes decide a number is a solution because it "looks right" or because it appeared in the problem. The test does not care about looks. For 3x + 2 = 17, the number 17 is in the problem, but 3(17) + 2 = 53, not 17. The number 5 is not in the problem, but 3(5) + 2 = 17, so 5 is the solution. Always substitute and compare the two sides before you trust an answer.

look.title: Test Three Numbers
look.text: The equation is 3x + 2 = 17. Try x = 4: 3(4) + 2 = 14, not 17. Try x = 5: 3(5) + 2 = 17, true. Try x = 6: 3(6) + 2 = 20, not 17. Only one of the three works.
look.prompt: Now test 4, 5 and 6 in 4x − 1 = 19. Which one is the solution, and how do you know?

check.q: Which value is a solution of 4x − 6 = 18?
check.why: 4(6) − 6 = 24 − 6 = 18, so 6 makes both sides equal. The others give 6, 14 and 26.

check.q: What does it mean for a number to be a solution of an equation?
choices: Substituting it makes both sides equal
It appears somewhere in the equation
It is the largest number that fits
It makes the left side equal zero
check.why: A solution makes the equation a true statement: after substituting, the left side and right side simplify to the same number.

check.q: Is 7 a solution of 2x + 5 = 19?
choices: No, because 7 is not in the equation
check.why: Substitute 7: 2(7) + 5 = 14 + 5 = 19, which equals the right side, so 7 is a solution.

lessons.title: Keeping the Balance
lessons.mainIdea: Whatever you do to one side of an equation, do to the other side, and the statement stays true.
reading: Picture a balance scale that is level. Add 2 pounds to the left pan only and it tips. Add 2 pounds to both pans and it stays level. An equation works the same way. The *properties of equality* say you can add, subtract, multiply or divide both sides by the same number and the new equation has the same solution as the old one. That is the whole toolkit for solving. You use it to *isolate* the variable, which means getting it alone on one side.

Solve 3x + 7 = 22. The variable is wrapped in two operations: multiplied by 3, then 7 is added. Undo them in reverse order using *inverse operations*. First subtract 7 from both sides: 3x + 7 − 7 = 22 − 7, so 3x = 15. Then divide both sides by 3: x = 5. Check by substituting: 3(5) + 7 = 15 + 7 = 22. True. Notice the *coefficient* 3 was handled last, because it was applied to x first.

One more: x/4 − 2 = 3. Add 2 to both sides: x/4 = 5. Multiply both sides by 4: x = 20. Check: 20/4 − 2 = 5 − 2 = 3. The most common mistake is doing the step on one side only, writing 3x = 22 − 7 but then forgetting the 7 was also on the left. Another is dividing only one term, turning 3x + 7 = 22 into x + 7 = 22/3. Every operation touches the whole of both sides.

look.title: The Text Message Bill
look.text: A phone plan costs $45 a month plus $0.10 for each text over the limit. One month the bill is $52.50. Let t be the number of extra texts: 45 + 0.10t = 52.50. Subtract 45 from both sides: 0.10t = 7.50. Divide both sides by 0.10: t = 75. Check: 45 + 0.10(75) = 45 + 7.50 = 52.50.
look.prompt: The next month's bill is $61.20. Set up the same kind of equation and find the number of extra texts.

check.q: Solve 5x − 8 = 27.
check.why: Add 8 to both sides: 5x = 35. Divide by 5: x = 7. Check: 5(7) − 8 = 27. Forgetting to divide gives 35.

check.q: Solve x/3 + 4 = 10.
check.why: Subtract 4: x/3 = 6. Multiply by 3: x = 18. Check: 18/3 + 4 = 6 + 4 = 10. Adding 4 instead of subtracting it gives 14 × 3 = 42, a common slip.

check.q: What is the best first step to solve 2x + 9 = 25?
choices: Subtract 9 from the left side only
check.why: Undo the addition first: subtracting 9 from both sides gives 2x = 16, then dividing gives x = 8. Dividing first would force you to divide the 9 too.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Equations with Reasons
lessons.mainIdea: Simplify each side first, then collect the variable on one side, and name the reason for every step.
reading: Some equations have parentheses, several terms, and variables on both sides. Solve 4(x − 3) + 2x = 3x + 6. Start by cleaning up each side. The *distributive property* turns 4(x − 3) into 4x − 12, because the 4 multiplies both the x and the 3. Now the left side is 4x − 12 + 2x. Combine the *like terms* 4x and 2x to get 6x − 12. The equation is now 6x − 12 = 3x + 6.

Next, get all the x terms on one side. Subtract 3x from both sides: 3x − 12 = 6. Add 12 to both sides: 3x = 18. Divide both sides by 3: x = 6. Check in the original equation: 4(6 − 3) + 2(6) = 4(3) + 12 = 24, and 3(6) + 6 = 24. Both sides are 24, so x = 6 is correct. Writing the reason next to each step is called *justifying* it: distributive property, combine like terms, subtraction property of equality, addition property, division property.

Two mistakes cause most wrong answers here. The first is distributing to only the first term, writing 4(x − 3) as 4x − 3. Try it with numbers: 4(5 − 3) = 8, but 4(5) − 3 = 17, so those are not the same. The second is moving a term across the equals sign without changing its sign. Subtracting 3x from the right side means subtracting 3x from the left side too. Justifying each step forces you to notice both errors.

words.d: a(b + c) = ab + ac; the number outside multiplies every term inside
terms with the same variable part, such as 4x and 2x, which can be combined
state the property or rule that makes a step legal

look.title: Every Step, One Reason
look.text: Solve 5(2x + 1) − 3x = 2x + 30. Distribute: 10x + 5 − 3x = 2x + 30. Combine like terms: 7x + 5 = 2x + 30. Subtract 2x from both sides: 5x + 5 = 30. Subtract 5: 5x = 25. Divide by 5: x = 5. Check: 5(11) − 15 = 40 and 2(5) + 30 = 40.
look.prompt: Solve 3(x + 4) − x = x + 20 the same way, writing the reason beside each line. What do you get, and does it check?

check.why: Distribute: 3x + 6 = 2x + 11. Subtract 2x: x + 6 = 11. Subtract 6: x = 5. Writing 3x + 2 instead of 3x + 6 gives the wrong answer 9.

check.q: Which property justifies going from 2x + 6 = 14 to 2x = 8?
check.why: Six was subtracted from both sides, which the subtraction property of equality allows without changing the solution.

check.q: Solve 7x − 4 = 3x + 20.
check.why: Subtract 3x: 4x − 4 = 20. Add 4: 4x = 24. Divide: x = 6. Check: 7(6) − 4 = 38 and 3(6) + 20 = 38. Adding 3x instead of subtracting gives 24/10 = 2.4.

lessons.title: Rearranging a Formula
lessons.mainIdea: A formula with several letters is solved the same way as any equation: undo operations until the letter you want stands alone.
reading: The perimeter of a rectangle is P = 2l + 2w. Usually you know the length and width and want P. But a fence builder often knows the total fencing and the length, and needs the width. A formula with more than one letter is a *literal equation*, and you can *solve for* any letter in it. Treat every other letter as if it were a known number.

Try it with numbers first. If P = 50 and l = 15, then 50 = 2(15) + 2w, so 50 = 30 + 2w. Subtract 30 from both sides: 20 = 2w. Divide by 2: w = 10. Now do the identical steps with letters. Start with P = 2l + 2w. Subtract 2l from both sides: P − 2l = 2w. Divide both sides by 2: w = (P − 2l)/2. Plug in P = 50 and l = 15 to see it give the same 10. The letter version is a new *formula* you can reuse for any fence.

Jasmine's fertilizer rule was pounds = 0.003 × A. To solve for A, divide both sides by 0.003: A = pounds/0.003. Six pounds covers 6/0.003 = 2,000 square feet. The classic error in rearranging is dividing only part of one side. From P − 2l = 2w, some students write w = P − 2l/2, which divides only the 2l. Parentheses matter: the whole expression P − 2l is divided by 2.

words.d: an equation with two or more letters, such as P = 2l + 2w
a rule written as an equation that relates quantities, like A = lw
rearrange an equation so a chosen variable is alone on one side

look.title: Distance, Rate and Time
look.text: The distance formula is d = rt. A CTA bus averaging 30 miles per hour that needs to cover 45 miles: 45 = 30t. Divide both sides by 30: t = 1.5 hours. In letters, dividing both sides of d = rt by r gives t = d/r. The same rearrangement works for a car, a walker or a train.
look.prompt: Solve d = rt for r. Then use your formula to find the speed of a runner who covers 12 miles in 1.5 hours.

check.q: Solve A = lw for w.
check.why: The width is multiplied by l, so divide both sides by l: w = A/l. For example, a 24-square-foot rug 6 feet long is 24/6 = 4 feet wide.

check.q: Solve y = mx + b for x.
check.why: Subtract b from both sides: y − b = mx. Divide both sides by m: x = (y − b)/m. The whole difference y − b is divided by m.

check.q: Using P = 2l + 2w with P = 36 and l = 10, what is w?
check.why: 36 = 20 + 2w, so 2w = 16 and w = 8. Check: 2(10) + 2(8) = 36. Forgetting to divide by 2 gives 16.

lessons.title: Temperature and Other Conversions
lessons.mainIdea: A conversion formula can be run in either direction once you solve it for the other variable.
reading: Weather in Chicago is reported in degrees *Fahrenheit*, but science class and most of the world use *Celsius*. The two scales are linked by F = (9/5)C + 32. Water freezes at 0 °C, and the formula gives (9/5)(0) + 32 = 32 °F. Water boils at 100 °C: (9/5)(100) + 32 = 180 + 32 = 212 °F. A warm 25 °C day becomes (9/5)(25) + 32 = 45 + 32 = 77 °F.

To go the other way, solve for C. Start with F = (9/5)C + 32. Subtract 32 from both sides: F − 32 = (9/5)C. Multiply both sides by 5/9, which undoes multiplying by 9/5: C = (5/9)(F − 32). Test it on a hot summer afternoon of 86 °F: 86 − 32 = 54, and (5/9)(54) = 30, so 86 °F is 30 °C. A cold January morning of −4 °F: −4 − 32 = −36, and (5/9)(−36) = −20, so −4 °F is −20 °C. Both formulas are *equivalent*; they describe the same relationship.

The order of operations trap here is subtracting 32 after multiplying. (5/9)(86) − 32 = 47.8 − 32 = 15.8, which is wrong. The 32 is added last in the forward formula, so it must be removed first when going backward. Whenever you rearrange a formula, test your new version with one pair of values you already trust, such as 0 °C and 32 °F.

words.d: the temperature scale used in U.S. weather reports; water freezes at 32 °F
the temperature scale used in science; water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C
two equations or formulas that describe exactly the same relationship

look.title: Celsius to Fahrenheit
look.cite: computed from the standard formula F = (9/5)C + 32
look.prompt: Each 10 °C step adds the same number of °F. What is that number, and where does it come from in the formula?

check.q: Convert 50 °F to Celsius.
check.why: 50 − 32 = 18, and (5/9)(18) = 10. Stopping after subtracting gives 18; using the forward formula gives 122.

check.q: Convert 15 °C to Fahrenheit.
check.why: (9/5)(15) = 27, then 27 + 32 = 59. Forgetting to multiply gives 47; forgetting to add 32 gives 27.

check.q: Which is F = (9/5)C + 32 correctly solved for C?
check.why: Subtract 32 first, then multiply by 5/9. Check with 212 °F: (5/9)(180) = 100 °C, the boiling point.

lessons.title: Absolute Value Equations
lessons.mainIdea: An absolute value equation usually has two solutions, one on each side of the center point.
reading: The *absolute value* of a number is its *distance* from zero on the number line, ignoring direction. So |5| = 5 and |−5| = 5. That means the equation |x| = 5 has two solutions, 5 and −5, because two numbers sit five units from zero. The equation |x − 3| = 5 asks which numbers are 5 units from 3. Split it into two ordinary equations: x − 3 = 5 gives x = 8, and x − 3 = −5 gives x = −2. Check: |8 − 3| = 5 and |−2 − 3| = |−5| = 5.

If the absolute value is not alone, isolate it first. Solve 3|x| + 2 = 14. Subtract 2: 3|x| = 12. Divide by 3: |x| = 4, so x = 4 or x = −4. Now try |2x + 1| = 7. Case one: 2x + 1 = 7, so 2x = 6 and x = 3. Case two: 2x + 1 = −7, so 2x = −8 and x = −4. Check the second: |2(−4) + 1| = |−7| = 7. Both work.

A distance can never be negative, so |x| + 5 = 2 has no solution at all: it would need |x| = −3. Absolute value shows up in manufacturing as *tolerance*. A part must measure 50 millimeters, give or take 0.2 millimeters. The acceptable extremes solve |m − 50| = 0.2, giving m = 50.2 and m = 49.8. The common mistake is forgetting the second case and reporting only the positive answer.

words.d: the distance of a number from zero, written |x|; it is never negative
how far apart two numbers are on the number line, always zero or positive
how far a measurement may be from its target and still be accepted

look.title: Five Units from Seven
look.text: |x − 7| = 3 asks for the numbers that are 3 units away from 7. Going up: x − 7 = 3, so x = 10. Going down: x − 7 = −3, so x = 4. On a number line, 4 and 10 sit on either side of 7, each 3 steps away.
look.prompt: Write an absolute value equation whose solutions are 2 and 12. What is the center, and what is the distance?

check.q: What are the solutions of |x + 2| = 6?
check.why: x + 2 = 6 gives x = 4; x + 2 = −6 gives x = −8. Check: |−8 + 2| = |−6| = 6. Dropping the second case gives only 4.

check.q: How many solutions does |x| + 5 = 2 have?
check.why: Subtracting 5 gives |x| = −3. A distance cannot be negative, so no number works.

check.q: Solve |3x − 6| = 12.

lessons.title: Inequalities Show a Range
lessons.mainIdea: An inequality is solved like an equation, but its solution is a whole range of numbers, shown on a number line.
reading: An *inequality* compares two sides with <, >, ≤ or ≥ instead of an equals sign. The statement x + 4 > 9 is true for x = 6, x = 10, x = 5.5 and infinitely many other values. All of those values together form the *solution set*. To find it, use the same balancing moves as with equations. Subtract 4 from both sides: x > 5. Every number greater than 5 works, and 5 itself does not.

Solve 2x − 3 ≤ 11. Add 3 to both sides: 2x ≤ 14. Divide by 2: x ≤ 7. Check with one number inside the range, say x = 0: 2(0) − 3 = −3, and −3 ≤ 11 is true. Check one number outside, say x = 10: 2(10) − 3 = 17, and 17 ≤ 11 is false. Checking both an inside and an outside value catches a wrong direction.

Draw the solution on a *number line*. The *boundary* number, 7, gets a closed dot because ≤ includes it, and an arrow points left toward all smaller numbers. For x > 5 the boundary 5 gets an open circle, because 5 is not included, and the arrow points right. The picture is the answer; a single number is not.

words.d: a statement comparing two sides with <, >, ≤ or ≥
every value that makes the inequality true
a line with numbers in order, used to picture a solution set
the number where the solution set starts or stops

look.title: How Many Rides
look.text: You load $20 onto a transit card. Each ride costs $2.50. The number of rides r must satisfy 2.50r ≤ 20. Divide both sides by 2.50: r ≤ 8. You can take up to 8 rides. The solution set is the whole numbers from 0 to 8, because you cannot take part of a ride.
look.prompt: Suppose the card already has $4.25 on it before you load $20. Write and solve the new inequality.

check.q: Solve 3x + 5 < 20.
check.why: Subtract 5: 3x < 15. Divide by 3: x < 5. Check x = 0: 5 < 20 is true. Forgetting to divide gives x < 15.

check.q: Which value is in the solution set of x − 4 ≥ 2?
check.why: Adding 4 gives x ≥ 6, and 6 is included because of the ≥. Check: 6 − 4 = 2, and 2 ≥ 2 is true.

check.q: How is x ≤ 7 drawn on a number line?
choices: Open circle at 7, arrow to the right
Closed dot at 7, arrow to the left
Closed dot at 7, arrow to the right
Open circle at 7, arrow to the left
check.why: The ≤ includes 7, so the dot is closed, and the solutions are smaller than 7, so the arrow points left.

lessons.title: When the Sign Flips
lessons.mainIdea: Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.
reading: Start with a true statement: 2 < 5. Multiply both sides by −1. You get −2 and −5, and on the number line −2 is to the right of −5, so −2 > −5. The direction changed. Multiplying or dividing by a *negative coefficient* flips every number to the other side of zero and swaps the order. So the rule: whenever you multiply or divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number, *reverse* the sign.

Solve −3x + 4 ≥ 19. Subtract 4 from both sides: −3x ≥ 15. Now divide both sides by −3 and reverse the sign: x ≤ −5. Check with x = −6: −3(−6) + 4 = 18 + 4 = 22, and 22 ≥ 19 is true. Check with x = 0: 0 + 4 = 4, and 4 ≥ 19 is false. The inside value works and the outside value fails, so x ≤ −5 is right.

You can avoid the flip entirely by moving the variable to the other side. From −3x + 4 ≥ 19, add 3x to both sides: 4 ≥ 19 + 3x. Subtract 19: −15 ≥ 3x. Divide by positive 3: −5 ≥ x, which is the same *equivalent inequality* x ≤ −5. The common mistake is flipping at the wrong moment, such as when subtracting a negative number. Adding and subtracting never flip the sign; only multiplying or dividing by a negative does.

words.d: a variable multiplied by a negative number, like −3x
switch < to > or ≤ to ≥ (and back)
an inequality with exactly the same solution set as another

look.title: Two Roads, Same Answer
look.text: Solve 8 − 2x > 14. Road one: subtract 8 to get −2x > 6, then divide by −2 and flip: x < −3. Road two: add 2x to both sides to get 8 > 14 + 2x, subtract 14 to get −6 > 2x, divide by 2: −3 > x, which is x < −3. Check x = −4: 8 − 2(−4) = 16 > 14. True.
look.prompt: Solve 5 − 3x ≤ 20 both ways. Do you get the same answer? Which road do you prefer, and why?

check.q: Solve −4x < 12.
check.why: Divide both sides by −4 and reverse the sign: x > −3. Check x = 0: 0 < 12 is true, so 0 must be in the set.

check.q: Solve 5 − x ≥ 2.
check.why: Subtract 5: −x ≥ −3. Multiply by −1 and flip: x ≤ 3. Check x = 0: 5 ≥ 2 is true.

check.q: Which step requires reversing the inequality sign?
check.why: Only multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the sign. Adding or subtracting any number, positive or negative, does not.

lessons.title: Compound Inequalities
lessons.mainIdea: A compound inequality joins two conditions with 'and' or 'or', and you solve every part at once.
reading: A refrigerator should stay between 34 °F and 40 °F. That is two conditions at once: T ≥ 34 and T ≤ 40. Written as one *compound inequality*, it is 34 ≤ T ≤ 40. The solution is the *intersection*, the numbers that satisfy both parts, which forms an *interval* on the number line from 34 to 40 with closed dots at both ends.

Solve −2 < x + 3 ≤ 6. There are three parts, and whatever you do must be done to all three. Subtract 3 from every part: −5 < x ≤ 3. The solution is every number greater than −5 and at most 3. Check x = 0, which is inside: −2 < 3 ≤ 6, true. Check x = 5, outside: −2 < 8 ≤ 6 is false because 8 is not ≤ 6. A frequent error is subtracting 3 from only the middle and the right, leaving −2 unchanged.

An 'or' inequality is different. Solve 2x − 1 < −7 or 3x + 2 > 11. Handle each separately: 2x < −6 gives x < −3, and 3x > 9 gives x > 3. The solution is the *union*: x < −3 or x > 3, two arrows pointing away from each other with a gap between −3 and 3. Numbers like 0 are not solutions. With 'and' you keep only what both parts share; with 'or' you keep everything either part allows.

words.d: two inequalities joined by 'and' or 'or'
the values that satisfy both parts of an 'and' inequality
the values that satisfy at least one part of an 'or' inequality
a stretch of the number line between two boundaries

look.title: Three Parts at Once
look.text: Solve 1 ≤ 2x − 3 ≤ 9. Add 3 to all three parts: 4 ≤ 2x ≤ 12. Divide all three parts by 2: 2 ≤ x ≤ 6. Check the middle value x = 4: 2(4) − 3 = 5, and 1 ≤ 5 ≤ 9 is true. Check x = 7: 2(7) − 3 = 11, and 11 ≤ 9 is false.
look.prompt: Solve −4 < 3x + 2 < 14. Then name one whole number that is a solution and one that is not.

check.why: Subtract 2 from all three parts: −3 ≤ 3x < 9. Divide by 3: −1 ≤ x < 3. Leaving out the division gives −3 ≤ x < 9.

check.q: Which number satisfies x < −2 or x > 4?
check.why: −5 is less than −2, so it satisfies the first part. 0 and 3 sit in the gap, and 4 is not greater than 4.

check.q: How is 'x ≥ 3 and x ≤ 8' written as one inequality?
check.why: Both conditions hold at once, so x sits between 3 and 8 including both ends: 3 ≤ x ≤ 8.

lessons.title: Writing Equations from Situations
lessons.mainIdea: To model a situation, define a variable, translate the words into an equation, solve it, and say what the number means.
reading: A gym charges $25 to join and $15 per month. Someone has paid $130 in total. How many months have they been a member? A *model* is an equation that captures the situation. First *define the variable*: let m be the number of months. The join fee is paid once and the monthly fee is paid m times, so 25 + 15m = 130. Subtract 25: 15m = 105. Divide by 15: m = 7. Finally *interpret*: they have been a member for 7 months. Check: 25 + 15(7) = 25 + 105 = 130.

Number puzzles use the same steps. Three consecutive integers add up to 48. Let n be the smallest. The next two are n + 1 and n + 2. The equation is n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 48, which simplifies to 3n + 3 = 48. Subtract 3: 3n = 45. Divide: n = 15. The integers are 15, 16 and 17, and 15 + 16 + 17 = 48.

Watch the key phrases. 'Twice a number decreased by 7' is 2n − 7, not 2(n − 7); the decrease happens after the doubling. 'Seven less than a number' is n − 7, not 7 − n. If the wording is unclear, plug in an easy number and see which expression matches what the sentence says. Then, after solving, always read your answer back into the story to see whether it makes sense.

words.d: an equation or inequality that represents a real situation
state in words exactly what the letter stands for, including units
explain what the solved number means in the original situation

look.title: Tickets Plus a Fee
look.text: Four concert tickets plus a single $12 service fee cost $172 in total. Let t be the price of one ticket: 4t + 12 = 172. Subtract 12: 4t = 160. Divide by 4: t = 40. Each ticket is $40. Check: 4(40) + 12 = 172.
look.prompt: Six tickets to a different show plus a $15 fee cost $195. Write the equation, solve it and state the ticket price.

check.q: A gym charges $25 to join and $15 per month. A member has paid $175. How many months is that?
Which equation says 'twice a number decreased by 7 is 19'?
check.why: Double the number first, then subtract 7: 2n − 7 = 19. Solving gives n = 13, and 2(13) − 7 = 19.

check.q: Two consecutive even integers add to 54. What are they?
check.why: Let n be the first: n + (n + 2) = 54, so 2n = 52 and n = 26. The integers are 26 and 28, and 26 + 28 = 54.

lessons.title: Limits Become Inequalities
lessons.mainIdea: Words like 'at most', 'at least' and 'no more than' signal an inequality, and the answer is a range that may need rounding.
reading: A freight elevator is rated for 2,000 pounds. A cart weighing 180 pounds is already inside, and each worker weighs about 150 pounds. How many workers can ride? The limit is a *constraint*, and 'rated for' means the total must be *at most* 2,000. Let p be the number of workers: 180 + 150p ≤ 2000. Subtract 180: 150p ≤ 1820. Divide by 150: p ≤ 12.13. You cannot have 0.13 of a person, so at most 12 workers can ride. Rounding up to 13 would break the limit: 180 + 150(13) = 2,130.

A club needs to raise *at least* $500 and has $124 so far. It sells candles for $8 each. Let c be the number of candles: 124 + 8c ≥ 500. Subtract 124: 8c ≥ 376. Divide by 8: c ≥ 47. They must sell 47 or more candles. Check: 124 + 8(47) = 124 + 376 = 500 exactly, so 47 just reaches the goal and 46 falls short at 492.

Translate the phrases carefully. 'At most 30' and 'no more than 30' both mean ≤ 30. 'At least 30' and 'no fewer than 30' both mean ≥ 30. 'More than 30' is strictly > 30. After solving, decide which numbers are actually *feasible*: whole numbers for people or candles, and never negative. A model with a solution like p ≤ 12.13 is telling you 12, not 12.13, and not 13.

words.d: a limit the situation places on the variable, such as a weight capacity
no more than; translates to ≤
no fewer than; translates to ≥
a value that is allowed by every constraint and makes sense in the situation

look.title: Loading the Truck
look.text: A pickup can carry at most 1,200 pounds. It already holds 300 pounds of tools. Bags of soil weigh 40 pounds each. Let b be the number of bags: 300 + 40b ≤ 1200. Subtract 300: 40b ≤ 900. Divide by 40: b ≤ 22.5. Since half a bag is not sold, the truck can take 22 bags. Check: 300 + 40(22) = 1,180, under the limit.
look.prompt: If the tools are unloaded first, how many bags fit? Write and solve the new inequality.

check.q: Which inequality means 'no more than 30 people'?
check.why: 'No more than 30' allows 30 itself and anything smaller, which is x ≤ 30.

check.q: A club has $124 and sells candles for $8 each. How many must it sell to reach at least $500?
check.why: 124 + 8c ≥ 500 gives 8c ≥ 376 and c ≥ 47. Selling 46 gives only $492. Dividing 500 by 8 ignores the $124 already raised.

check.q: An elevator holds 2,000 pounds. A 180-pound cart is inside and workers average 150 pounds. How many workers can ride?
check.why: 180 + 150p ≤ 2000 gives p ≤ 12.13, so 12 workers. Thirteen would total 2,130 pounds, over the limit.

lessons.title: Units and Reasonableness
lessons.mainIdea: Carry the units through your work and compare the answer to a rough estimate before you trust it.
reading: Back to the fertilizer bag: 3 pounds for every 1,000 square feet. A bed 40 feet by 60 feet has area 40 ft × 60 ft = 2,400 square feet. The rate is 3 lb per 1,000 sq ft, so pounds = 2,400 sq ft × (3 lb / 1,000 sq ft) = 7.2 lb. Notice the square feet cancel and only pounds remain. This tracking of units is called *unit analysis*. If a student multiplied by 3 without dividing by 1,000, the answer would be 7,200, and the leftover units would be pound-square-feet, which is meaningless. The units flag the error.

An *estimate* catches errors too. Before computing, ask: is 2,400 square feet more or less than 1,000? It is a bit more than double, so the answer should be a bit more than double 3 pounds, roughly 6 to 8. An answer of 7.2 is *reasonable*; an answer of 720 or 0.72 is not. Estimating first takes ten seconds and saves a whole wrong page.

Time is the unit that trips people up most. A trip of 60 miles at 40 miles per hour takes 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5 hours. That is 1 hour and 30 minutes, not 1 hour and 50 minutes, because 0.5 hour × 60 minutes per hour = 30 minutes. Likewise 0.6 hour is 36 minutes. And some answers are impossible on their face: −3 tickets, 4.5 people, or a 90-year-old kindergartner. When the number is impossible, the model or the arithmetic is wrong, not the world.

words.d: tracking units through a calculation and canceling them like factors
a rough answer found quickly, used to judge whether the exact answer makes sense
an answer whose size and units fit the situation

look.title: Fertilizer for Different Beds
look.cite: example rate of 3 pounds per 1,000 square feet, a typical instruction on lawn fertilizer bags
look.prompt: Doubling the area doubles the pounds. Use the table to estimate the pounds for 3,300 square feet before you calculate it exactly.

check.q: How many minutes is 0.6 hour?
check.why: 0.6 × 60 minutes = 36 minutes. Reading 0.6 hour as '60 minutes' or as '6 minutes' is a common slip.

check.q: A bed is 30 feet by 50 feet. At 3 pounds per 1,000 square feet, how much fertilizer is needed?
check.why: Area is 30 × 50 = 1,500 sq ft, which is 1.5 thousands, so 1.5 × 3 = 4.5 pounds. An answer of 4,500 forgot to divide by 1,000.

check.q: Which answer should make you recheck your work?
check.why: A negative number of tickets is impossible, so either the equation or the arithmetic has an error. The other answers are all plausible.

review.q: Which value is a solution of 6x − 5 = 31?

review.why: Distribute: 2x − 8 = 3x − 15. Subtract 2x: −8 = x − 15. Add 15: x = 7. Check: 2(3) = 6 and 21 − 15 = 6.

review.q: Solve C = 2πr for r.
review.why: r is multiplied by 2π, so divide both sides by 2π: r = C/(2π).

review.q: What are the solutions of |x − 5| = 2?
review.why: x − 5 = 2 gives 7; x − 5 = −2 gives 3. Both numbers are 2 units from 5.

review.q: Solve −2x + 7 > 1.
review.why: Subtract 7: −2x > −6. Divide by −2 and reverse: x < 3. Check x = 0: 7 > 1 is true.

review.q: Solve 3 ≤ 2x + 1 ≤ 11.
review.why: Subtract 1 from all parts: 2 ≤ 2x ≤ 10. Divide by 2: 1 ≤ x ≤ 5.

review.q: A plumber charges $60 to visit plus $45 per hour. The bill is $240. How many hours did the job take?
review.why: 60 + 45h = 240, so 45h = 180 and h = 4. Dividing 240 by 45 ignores the visit fee.

review.q: A van seats at most 12 people. Two adults must ride. Which inequality gives the number of students s?
review.why: The two adults plus the students cannot exceed 12 seats: 2 + s ≤ 12, so s ≤ 10.

chapters.title: Functions and Linear Models
chapters.bigQuestion: When a rule turns one number into another, how do you read, write and use that rule to predict?

story.title: Taxi Fare, Cell Data and the Meaning of f(3)
story.kicker: The same input, 3, gives two different answers, and both are right, because the rules are different.
paragraphs: Darnell steps out of Union Station in downtown Chicago and gets into a taxi. The sticker on the window lists the rates (for this story we will use round example numbers): $3 as soon as the meter starts, plus $2 for every mile. He watches the meter. At the start it reads $3.00. After one mile, $5.00. After two miles, $7.00. He realizes he can predict the next number before it appears: after three miles it will read $9.00.

In his head Darnell writes the rule the meter is following: fare = 3 + 2 × miles. If he calls the rule f and lets x be the miles, then f(x) = 2x + 3. The symbol f(3) means "put 3 into the rule f." It comes out to 2(3) + 3 = 9. So f(3) = 9 says that a 3-mile ride costs $9. It is not f times 3. It is a question and its answer: what does the rule give for an input of 3?

While he rides, a text arrives about his cell plan: $20 a month plus $8 for each gigabyte of data. That is a different rule, so he gives it a different name: d(g) = 8g + 20. Now d(3) = 8(3) + 20 = 44. Same input, 3, but a different rule, so a different output, $44 for 3 gigabytes. The letter in front tells you which machine you are feeding the number into.

The taxi stops after 4 miles and the meter reads $11.00. Darnell checks: f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11. He tips and gets out thinking about how many things in his day work this way. Minutes on the treadmill turn into calories. Hours worked turn into pay. Weeks of saving turn into a balance. Each one is a rule with a name, an input and exactly one output. Learning to read and write those rules is what this chapter is for.
story.think: Darnell's friend says f(3) = 9 means 'f times 3 is 9, so f must be 3.' What has she misunderstood, and how would you explain it using the taxi meter?

lessons.title: Inputs and Outputs
lessons.mainIdea: A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input.
reading: A taxi meter is a machine: you feed in a number of miles and it gives back a fare. Feed in 1 mile, get $5. Feed in 2 miles, get $7. Feed in 3 miles, get $9. No matter how many times you feed in 3 miles, the meter gives back $9, never $8 and never $10. That is the key property of a *function*: every *input* is matched with exactly one *output*. The set of miles is the input, the set of fares is the output, and the rule connecting them is the function.

Any set of matched pairs is called a *relation*, but not every relation is a function. Suppose a table listed 2 miles → $5 and also 2 miles → $7. The same input has two different outputs, so the table is not a function; the meter would be broken. On the other hand, two different inputs can share an output. A rule that charges $10 for any ride under a mile, so that 0.3 miles → $10 and 0.8 miles → $10, is still a function, because each input still has only one answer.

On a graph, the input is on the horizontal axis and the output on the vertical axis. If any vertical line crosses the graph twice, then one input has two outputs and the graph is not a function. This is the vertical line test. A straight slanted line always passes the test. A circle fails, because a vertical line through its middle hits the top and the bottom.

words.d: a rule that assigns exactly one output to each input
the number you put into a rule, such as the miles of a taxi ride
the number the rule gives back, such as the fare
any set of input-output pairs, whether or not it is a function

look.title: The Taxi Meter Table
look.cite: example taxi rates of $3 to start plus $2 per mile, used throughout this chapter
look.prompt: Every input has exactly one fare, so the table is a function. What fare would the rule give for 7 miles, and how do you know?

check.q: Which set of pairs is NOT a function?
check.why: The input 2 is matched with both 5 and 7, so one input has two outputs. Sharing an output, as in the second choice, is allowed.

check.q: Using the taxi table, what is the fare for a 3-mile ride?
check.why: The rule is $3 plus $2 per mile: 3 + 2(3) = 9. The table row for 3 miles confirms $9.

check.q: A graph passes the vertical line test when…
choices: every vertical line touches it once at most
it goes up from left to right
check.why: One input with two outputs would show as a vertical line hitting the graph twice. Touching at most once means each input has one output.

lessons.title: Reading f(3)
lessons.mainIdea: f(3) means the output of rule f when the input is 3; it is a question and its answer, not a product.
reading: *Function notation* gives a rule a name. The taxi rule is f(x) = 2x + 3. Read it as "f of x equals 2x plus 3." The letter f is the name, x is the *input value*, and 2x + 3 is what the rule does. To *evaluate* f(3), replace every x with 3: f(3) = 2(3) + 3 = 9. In the story, that means a 3-mile ride costs $9. The parentheses do not mean multiplication here. f(3) is not f × 3.

The notation runs backward too. If someone asks, "How far can I ride for $15?" you are solving f(x) = 15. Write 2x + 3 = 15, subtract 3 to get 2x = 12, and divide to get x = 6. A $15 ride is 6 miles. Notice the difference between the two questions: f(6) asks for the output when the input is 6 (answer: 15), while f(x) = 15 asks which input gives an output of 15 (answer: 6).

Be careful with expressions inside and outside the parentheses. f(x + 1) means put x + 1 into the rule: f(3 + 1) = f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11. But f(x) + 1 means find f(x) first and then add 1: f(3) + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10. Different rules get different names so they do not get mixed up: the cell data rule is d(g) = 8g + 20, and d(3) = 44 while f(3) = 9.

words.d: writing a rule with a name and its input, like f(x) = 2x + 3
find the output of a function for a specific input
the number placed inside the parentheses, replacing the variable

look.title: Four Questions About g
look.text: Let g(x) = 5x − 4. Then g(2) = 5(2) − 4 = 6. And g(0) = 0 − 4 = −4. And g(−1) = −5 − 4 = −9. Now solve g(x) = 21: 5x − 4 = 21, so 5x = 25 and x = 5. Three questions asked for outputs; the last asked for an input.
look.prompt: Let h(x) = 3x + 7. Find h(4), h(−2) and the value of x that makes h(x) = 25.

check.q: If f(x) = 3x − 2, what is f(4)?
check.why: f(4) = 3(4) − 2 = 12 − 2 = 10. Forgetting the −2 gives 12.

check.q: For the taxi rule, what does f(3) = 9 mean?
choices: f is 3 and the fare is 9
check.why: The input 3 is the miles and the output 9 is the fare: riding 3 miles costs $9.

check.q: If h(x) = 4x + 1, for what x does h(x) = 29?
check.why: 4x + 1 = 29, so 4x = 28 and x = 7. Check: h(7) = 28 + 1 = 29. Evaluating h(29) instead gives 117.

lessons.title: Domain and Range
lessons.mainIdea: The domain is every input a function allows, and the range is every output it can produce.
reading: The cell plan rule d(g) = 8g + 20 works fine on paper for g = 1,000, but the plan caps data at 10 gigabytes. So the inputs that actually make sense run from 0 to 10. That set of allowed inputs is the *domain*: 0 ≤ g ≤ 10. Feed the smallest and largest inputs through the rule to find the outputs: d(0) = 20 and d(10) = 8(10) + 20 = 100. Since the rule rises steadily, every cost from $20 to $100 is possible. That set of outputs is the *range*: 20 ≤ d ≤ 100.

Some functions accept only certain kinds of numbers. Movie tickets cost $12 each, so c(n) = 12n, but n must be a whole number: you cannot buy 2.5 tickets. If the website allows up to 6 tickets, the domain is {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} and the range is {0, 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72}. A domain made of separate values like this is *discrete*, and its graph is dots. The taxi domain, miles ≥ 0, is *continuous*, because a ride can be 2.37 miles, and its graph is a solid line.

Domain and range often get swapped, so anchor them to the axes: domain is the set of x-values (horizontal), range is the set of y-values (vertical). When a problem gives a context, use it. Time cannot be negative, tickets come in whole numbers, and a plan has a cap. The context shrinks the domain, and the rule then decides the range.

words.d: the set of all inputs a function accepts
the set of all outputs a function produces
made of separate values, like counts of tickets; graphed as dots
including every value in an interval, like miles or minutes; graphed as a line

look.title: Tickets, Up to Six
look.text: Tickets cost $12 each and the site sells at most 6 per order, so c(n) = 12n with domain {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. The outputs are 0, 12, 24, 36, 48, 60 and 72 dollars. There is no order that costs $30, because 30 is not 12 times a whole number.
look.prompt: A parking lot charges $4 per hour for up to 8 hours, and charges by the whole hour. Write the function and give its domain and range.

check.q: For d(g) = 8g + 20 with domain 0 ≤ g ≤ 10, what is the range?
check.why: d(0) = 20 and d(10) = 100, and the rule rises steadily, so the outputs run from 20 to 100.

check.q: Which quantity has a discrete domain?
choices: Gallons of water in a tank
check.why: Tickets come in whole numbers only, so the inputs are separate values. Minutes, miles and gallons can take any value in an interval.

check.q: What is a sensible domain for the taxi fare function f(x) = 2x + 3?
check.why: Miles cannot be negative, but a ride can be any length such as 2.4 miles, so the domain is x ≥ 0.

lessons.title: Slope as a Rate of Change
lessons.mainIdea: Slope is the change in output divided by the change in input, and in a story it is a rate.
reading: On the taxi graph, the point (1, 5) means 1 mile costs $5 and (4, 11) means 4 miles cost $11. Between them the fare rose by 11 − 5 = 6 dollars while the miles rose by 4 − 1 = 3. The *slope* is the vertical change divided by the horizontal change: 6/3 = 2. In the story that is $2 per mile, the *rate of change*. The vertical change is often called the *rise* and the horizontal change the *run*, so slope = rise/run.

The formula for two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is slope = (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1). For (2, 7) and (5, 16): (16 − 7)/(5 − 2) = 9/3 = 3. Order does not matter as long as you are consistent. Going the other way, (7 − 16)/(2 − 5) = −9/−3 = 3, the same. The mistake to avoid is mixing the orders: (16 − 7)/(2 − 5) = 9/−3 = −3, which is wrong.

Slope can be negative. A tank starts with 500 gallons and holds 400 gallons after 4 minutes: (400 − 500)/(4 − 0) = −100/4 = −25. The tank loses 25 gallons per minute. For a linear function the slope is the same between any two points, which is exactly what makes it linear. For a curve, the same calculation gives the average rate of change over that interval, which is why the formula is worth memorizing.

words.d: the steepness of a line: change in y divided by change in x
how much the output changes for each one-unit change of input
the vertical change between two points on a graph
the horizontal change between two points on a graph

look.title: A Draining Tank
look.cite: table of values from the function g(t) = 500 − 25t
look.prompt: Pick any two rows and compute the slope. Then pick two different rows. Why do you get the same number each time?

check.q: What is the slope of the line through (1, 4) and (3, 10)?
check.why: (10 − 4)/(3 − 1) = 6/2 = 3. Forgetting to divide by the run gives 6.

check.q: A tank has 500 gallons at 0 minutes and 350 gallons at 6 minutes. What is the rate of change?
check.why: (350 − 500)/(6 − 0) = −150/6 = −25. The tank loses 25 gallons each minute, so the rate is negative.

check.q: In the taxi function, the slope 2 stands for…
check.why: Slope is change in fare per change in miles: each extra mile adds $2. The starting fare is the y-intercept, 3.

lessons.title: Slope-Intercept Form
lessons.mainIdea: In y = mx + b, m is the rate of change and b is the starting value where the line crosses the y-axis.
reading: Every *linear function* can be written in *slope-intercept form*, y = mx + b. The number m is the slope, and b is the *y-intercept*, the output when the input is 0. In the cell plan d = 8g + 20, m = 8 means $8 per gigabyte and b = 20 means the bill is $20 before any data is used. That b is often called the *initial value* because it is where the story starts.

You can build the equation from two points. Say a bill was $28 for 1 GB and $52 for 4 GB, so the points are (1, 28) and (4, 52). Slope: (52 − 28)/(4 − 1) = 24/3 = 8. Now find b by substituting one point into y = 8x + b: 28 = 8(1) + b, so b = 20. The function is d = 8g + 20. Check with the other point: 8(4) + 20 = 52. It matches.

From a graph, read b where the line crosses the vertical axis, then count rise over run to a second clear point. The common mistake is swapping m and b: reading y = 3x + 5 as "starts at 3, goes up 5 each time." Remember that the number attached to x is the one that repeats with every step, and the lone number is paid once.

words.d: a function whose graph is a straight line; it has a constant rate of change
the equation y = mx + b, where m is the slope and b the y-intercept
the output when the input is 0; where the graph crosses the y-axis
the starting amount in a story, which appears as b in y = mx + b

look.title: Bikes by the Lake
look.text: A lakefront bike rental charges a flat $8 plus $6 per hour. The cost function is c(h) = 6h + 8. Three hours: c(3) = 18 + 8 = 26. The 8 is paid once (the intercept); the 6 is paid every hour (the slope).
look.prompt: A car-wash fundraiser starts with a $50 donation and earns $7 per car. Write the function, identify m and b, and find the total after 30 cars.

check.q: For y = −3x + 5, what are the slope and y-intercept?
check.why: The coefficient of x is the slope, −3, and the constant term is the y-intercept, 5.

check.q: Which equation gives the line through (2, 11) and (5, 20)?
In d = 8g + 20, what does the 20 represent?
choices: The bill before any data is used
check.why: When g = 0 the bill is 20, so 20 is the fixed monthly charge before data. The cost per gigabyte is 8.

lessons.title: Arithmetic Sequences as Functions
lessons.mainIdea: An arithmetic sequence is a linear function whose inputs are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, and so on.
reading: A stadium's first row has 20 seats, and each row behind it has 2 more: 20, 22, 24, 26, … A list where you add the same amount each time is an *arithmetic sequence*, and the amount added, here 2, is the *common difference*. Each number in the list is a *term*. Row 1 is term 1, row 2 is term 2. To find any term, notice that row n has taken n − 1 steps of size 2 from the first row: a(n) = 20 + 2(n − 1), which simplifies to a(n) = 2n + 18. Row 15 has a(15) = 30 + 18 = 48 seats.

Look at the sequence 5, 9, 13, 17, … The common difference is 4. The *explicit rule* is a(n) = 5 + 4(n − 1) = 4n + 1. Check: a(1) = 5, a(2) = 9, a(3) = 13. Then a(10) = 41. The same sequence has a *recursive rule*: a(1) = 5 and a(n) = a(n − 1) + 4, which says "start at 5 and keep adding 4." The recursive rule is easy to state but slow to use for a(100); the explicit rule gets there in one step.

The explicit rule a(n) = 4n + 1 is a linear function with slope 4 and intercept 1, but its domain is only the positive integers, so its graph is a row of dots on a line, not the line itself. The common difference is the slope. The usual error is writing a(n) = 5 + 4n, which starts at 9 instead of 5. Always test your rule on the first term before trusting it.

words.d: a list of numbers with the same amount added each time
the fixed amount added to get from one term to the next
one number in a sequence; a(3) is the third term
a formula that gives any term directly from its position n
a rule that gives the first term and how to get each term from the one before

look.title: Find the Twentieth Term
look.text: The sequence 7, 12, 17, 22, … has common difference 5. Explicit rule: a(n) = 7 + 5(n − 1) = 5n + 2. Test: a(1) = 7, a(2) = 12. Then a(20) = 100 + 2 = 102. Counting up by 5 twenty times would give the same answer, just more slowly.
look.prompt: Write the explicit rule for 4, 11, 18, 25, … and use it to find the 30th term.

check.q: What is the common difference of 3, 10, 17, 24, …?
check.why: 10 − 3 = 7, 17 − 10 = 7 and 24 − 17 = 7. The same 7 is added each time.

check.q: For the sequence 5, 9, 13, 17, …, what is the 10th term?
check.why: a(n) = 4n + 1, so a(10) = 41. Using 5 + 4n by mistake gives 45.

check.q: If a(1) = 6 and a(n) = a(n − 1) − 3, what is a(4)?
check.why: a(2) = 3, a(3) = 0, a(4) = −3. Three steps of −3 from 6 gives 6 − 9 = −3.

lessons.title: Key Features of a Graph
lessons.mainIdea: Intercepts, direction and zeros tell the story of a graph in a few numbers.
reading: A tank holds 500 gallons and drains at 25 gallons per minute, so y = 500 − 25x. Its graph crosses the vertical axis at 500: that is the *y-intercept*, the amount at time 0. It crosses the horizontal axis where y = 0. Solve 500 − 25x = 0: 25x = 500, so x = 20. That is the *x-intercept*, also called the *zero of a function*, and it means the tank is empty after 20 minutes.

The line falls from left to right, so the function is *decreasing*: every extra minute gives fewer gallons. A savings function like s(w) = 30w + 120 is *increasing*, because each week adds $30. Its y-intercept, 120, is the starting balance. Its zero would be at 30w + 120 = 0, so w = −4, but negative weeks are outside the domain, so the graph never reaches zero in the story.

A graph is also positive where it sits above the horizontal axis and negative where it sits below. For the tank, y is positive for 0 ≤ x < 20 and would be negative after that, which is impossible, so the sensible domain is 0 ≤ x ≤ 20. When you read any graph, ask four questions: where does it start (y-intercept), where does it hit zero (x-intercept), does it rise or fall (increasing or decreasing), and which inputs actually make sense (domain).

words.d: the point where a graph crosses the vertical axis; the output at input 0
the point where a graph crosses the horizontal axis; the input that gives output 0
an input value that makes the output 0; same as an x-intercept
rising from left to right; outputs grow as inputs grow
falling from left to right; outputs shrink as inputs grow

look.title: Reading a Savings Line
look.text: A student starts with $120 and saves $30 a week: s(w) = 30w + 120. The y-intercept 120 is the starting balance. The line rises, so it is increasing. After 10 weeks, s(10) = 300 + 120 = 420. Setting s(w) = 600 gives 30w = 480, so w = 16 weeks to reach $600.
look.prompt: Suppose instead the student starts with $500 and spends $40 a week. Write the function, find both intercepts, and say what each means.

check.q: What is the x-intercept of y = 500 − 25x?
check.why: Set y = 0: 500 − 25x = 0, so x = 20. The tank is empty after 20 minutes.

check.q: For the tank, what does the y-intercept 500 mean?
choices: The tank loses 500 gallons per minute
The tank holds 500 gallons at time 0
The tank is empty at 500 gallons
check.why: The y-intercept is the output when x = 0, so at the start the tank holds 500 gallons.

check.q: Which function is decreasing?
check.why: A negative slope means the line falls from left to right. The slope of y = −2x + 9 is −2.

lessons.title: Building a Model from Data
lessons.mainIdea: When a table's outputs change by the same amount each step, a linear model fits, and you can use it to predict.
reading: A bike rental posts these prices: 1 hour $14, 2 hours $20, 3 hours $26, 4 hours $32. Each extra hour adds 20 − 14 = 6, then 26 − 20 = 6, then 32 − 26 = 6. Constant differences mean a *linear model* fits. The slope is 6 dollars per hour. To find the intercept, step back one hour from (1, 14): 14 − 6 = 8. The model is c = 6h + 8, meaning an $8 flat fee plus $6 per hour. Check: 6(4) + 8 = 32.

A model earns its keep by making a *prediction*. For 7 hours, c = 6(7) + 8 = 50. That prediction lies just outside the table's range of 1 to 4 hours, which is called *extrapolating*. Predicting a value inside the table's range, such as 2.5 hours giving 6(2.5) + 8 = 23, is *interpolating* and is usually safer. Far extrapolation is risky: for 40 hours the model gives $248, but the shop probably switches to a daily rate long before that.

Real data rarely lines up perfectly. If the differences were 6, 7, 5 and 6, the pattern is still roughly linear and a line drawn through the middle of the points is a reasonable model. State the slope with its units, state what the intercept means, and say how far you trust the prediction. A model is a tool for the situation it came from, not a law of nature.

words.d: a linear function used to describe and predict a real situation
an output the model gives for an input you have not measured
predict for an input inside the range of the data you have
predict for an input outside the range of the data you have

look.title: Bike Rental Prices
look.cite: example price list invented for this lesson
look.prompt: Confirm the model c = 6h + 8 fits every row. Then use it to predict the cost of 8 hours and say whether that is interpolating or extrapolating.

check.q: Which model fits the rental table?
check.why: The differences are all 6, so the slope is 6. Then 14 = 6(1) + b gives b = 8.

check.q: Using c = 6h + 8, what is the cost for 7 hours?
check.why: 6(7) + 8 = 42 + 8 = 50. Forgetting the flat fee gives 42.

check.q: Predicting the cost of 40 hours from this table is…
choices: extrapolating, and risky because the pricing may change
check.why: 40 hours is far outside the 1-to-5-hour data, so it is extrapolation, and a shop likely charges a different daily rate.

lessons.title: Piecewise and Step Functions
lessons.mainIdea: A piecewise function uses different rules on different parts of its domain; a step function jumps between constant values.
reading: A downtown garage charges $5 for the first hour and $3 for each additional hour or part of an hour. One hour costs $5. Two hours cost $8. Two and a half hours also cost $11, because the half hour counts as a full extra hour. The graph is flat at $5 up to 1 hour, jumps to $8, stays flat, jumps to $11, and so on. A graph made of flat pieces with jumps is a *step function*. It is still a function: every parking time has exactly one price.

More generally, a *piecewise function* has a different rule on each *interval* of its domain. Overtime pay is a classic case: a worker earns $15 an hour for the first 40 hours and $22.50 an hour after that. So p(h) = 15h when h ≤ 40, and p(h) = 600 + 22.5(h − 40) when h > 40, where 600 is the pay for the first 40 hours. For a 44-hour week, use the second rule: 600 + 22.5(4) = 600 + 90 = 690.

To evaluate a piecewise function, first find which interval the input belongs to, then apply that rule only. Let f(x) = 2x for x < 3 and f(x) = x + 3 for x ≥ 3. Then f(2) = 4 because 2 < 3, and f(5) = 8 because 5 ≥ 3. The boundary matters: f(3) uses the second rule since 3 ≥ 3, so f(3) = 6. The common mistake is applying both rules or the wrong one at the boundary.

words.d: a function defined by different rules on different parts of its domain
a piecewise function whose pieces are all flat, so the graph looks like stairs
a stretch of inputs, such as 0 to 40 hours, where one rule applies

look.title: Shipping by Weight
look.text: A shipper charges $4 for packages up to 1 pound, $7 for more than 1 pound up to 3 pounds, and $10 for more than 3 pounds up to 5 pounds. A 2.4-pound box costs $7. A 3-pound box costs $7, because 3 is included in the middle interval. A 3.1-pound box costs $10.
look.prompt: Sketch the steps of this function. Where are the jumps, and which end of each step is included?

check.q: The garage charges $5 for the first hour and $3 per additional hour or part. What does 3.5 hours cost?
check.why: After the first hour, 2.5 more hours count as 3 additional hours: 5 + 3(3) = 14.

check.q: With $15 per hour up to 40 hours and $22.50 per hour beyond, what is the pay for 44 hours?
check.why: The first 40 hours earn 600; the 4 overtime hours earn 22.5(4) = 90; the total is 690.

check.q: If f(x) = 2x for x < 3 and f(x) = x + 3 for x ≥ 3, what is f(3)?
check.why: Since 3 ≥ 3, use the second rule: f(3) = 3 + 3 = 6. The first rule would only apply to inputs below 3.

lessons.title: Shifting and Stretching Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Adding to the output slides a graph up or down, adding to the input slides it sideways, and multiplying the output changes its steepness.
reading: Start with f(x) = 2x, the taxi rate without a starting fee. Now the company adds a $3 flag fee: g(x) = f(x) + 3 = 2x + 3. Every output is 3 more than before, so the whole line slides up 3 units. This is a *vertical shift*, one kind of *transformation*. At x = 0, 1 and 2, f gives 0, 2 and 4, while g gives 3, 5 and 7. Same slope, higher line.

Adding inside the parentheses changes the input instead. h(x) = f(x − 1) = 2(x − 1) = 2x − 2. To get the output f used to give at x = 1, you now must put in x = 2. The graph slides right 1 unit, a *horizontal shift*. Notice the direction: x − 1 moves right and x + 1 moves left, the opposite of what many people first guess. Check with a point: f(1) = 2, and h(2) = 2(2) − 2 = 2, so the point moved from (1, 2) to (2, 2).

Multiplying the output makes the line steeper or flatter. k(x) = 3·f(x) = 6x has slope 6 instead of 2, a *vertical stretch*. The intercept stays at 0, but each output is tripled: at x = 2, f gives 4 and k gives 12. Fastest way to see a transformation is a small table of three inputs. If every output changed by the same amount, it was a shift; if the outputs were multiplied, it was a stretch.

words.d: a change that moves or reshapes a graph in a predictable way
sliding a graph up or down by adding a number to every output
sliding a graph left or right by adding a number to the input
multiplying every output by a number, which changes a line's steepness

look.title: Three Rows, Three Functions
look.text: Let f(x) = x + 1. For x = 0, 1, 2: f gives 1, 2, 3. Then f(x) + 4 gives 5, 6, 7, each output up by 4. And 3·f(x) gives 3, 6, 9, each output tripled. The first change slides the line; the second tilts it.
look.prompt: Make the same three-row table for f(x) = 2x − 1, f(x) − 3 and 2·f(x). Which one has the same slope as f?

check.q: How does the graph of y = 2x + 5 compare with y = 2x?
check.why: Adding 5 to every output slides the line up 5 units; the slope 2 does not change.

check.q: If f(x) = 4x − 1, what is g(x) = f(x) − 3?
check.why: Subtract 3 from the whole output: 4x − 1 − 3 = 4x − 4. The slope stays 4.

check.q: Which change alters the slope of a line?
check.why: Multiplying outputs by 3 triples the rise for the same run, so the slope triples. Shifts move the line without tilting it.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Models
lessons.mainIdea: To compare two linear models, find where their outputs are equal, then see which is better on each side of that point.
reading: Two cell plans: Plan A charges $20 plus $8 per gigabyte, so A(g) = 8g + 20. Plan B charges $35 plus $5 per gigabyte, so B(g) = 5g + 35. Which is cheaper? Try 3 GB: A(3) = 44 and B(3) = 50, so A wins. Try 8 GB: A(8) = 84 and B(8) = 75, so B wins. Somewhere between 3 and 8 the plans must cost the same. That crossing is the *break-even point*.

To find it exactly, set the outputs equal: 8g + 20 = 5g + 35. Subtract 5g: 3g + 20 = 35. Subtract 20: 3g = 15. Divide: g = 5. Check: A(5) = 60 and B(5) = 60. Both plans cost $60 at 5 GB. On a graph, this is the *intersection point* (5, 60) where the two lines cross. Below 5 GB the lower-intercept plan A is cheaper; above 5 GB the lower-slope plan B is cheaper.

This is a good *comparison* habit: the plan with the smaller starting cost wins for small inputs, and the plan with the smaller rate wins for large inputs. The crossing point tells you where the advantage flips. Setting two rules equal and solving is the door into the next chapter, where two equations are solved together as a system.

words.d: the input where two models give the same output
the point where two graphs cross; both equations are true there
checking two models against each other to see which is better for a given input

look.title: Two Savers
look.text: Ana has $200 and saves $15 a week: 15w + 200. Ben has $80 and saves $25 a week: 25w + 80. Set them equal: 15w + 200 = 25w + 80. Subtract 15w: 200 = 10w + 80. Subtract 80: 120 = 10w, so w = 12. After 12 weeks both have 15(12) + 200 = 380 dollars. After that, Ben pulls ahead.
look.prompt: Who has more money after 6 weeks? After 20 weeks? Explain using the slopes and intercepts.

check.q: At how many gigabytes do Plan A (8g + 20) and Plan B (5g + 35) cost the same?
check.why: 8g + 20 = 5g + 35 gives 3g = 15, so g = 5. Both cost $60 there.

check.q: Which plan is cheaper at 2 GB?
check.why: A(2) = 16 + 20 = 36 and B(2) = 10 + 35 = 45, so Plan A is cheaper by $9.

check.q: Ana has $200 and saves $15 a week; Ben has $80 and saves $25 a week. When are they equal?

review.q: If f(x) = 5x − 7, what is f(3)?
review.why: f(3) = 5(3) − 7 = 15 − 7 = 8. Leaving off the −7 gives 15.

review.q: Which set of pairs is a function?
review.why: Each input appears once, so each has one output. Sharing the output 6 is fine. The other sets repeat an input with different outputs.

review.q: What is the slope of the line through (2, 3) and (6, 15)?
A plan costs $30 per month plus $4 per gigabyte. Which function gives the cost?
review.why: The $30 is paid once (intercept) and $4 repeats per gigabyte (slope): c(g) = 4g + 30.

review.q: What is the 12th term of the sequence 9, 14, 19, 24, …?
review.why: Common difference 5, so a(n) = 9 + 5(n − 1) = 5n + 4. Then a(12) = 60 + 4 = 64.

review.q: What is the x-intercept of y = 4x − 12?
review.why: Set y = 0: 4x − 12 = 0, so 4x = 12 and x = 3.

review.q: If f(x) = 3x, which function is f shifted down 2 units?
review.why: Shifting down subtracts 2 from every output: 3x − 2.

review.q: Movie tickets cost $12 each, up to 6 per order. What is the range of c(n) = 12n?
review.why: The domain is the whole numbers 0 through 6, so the outputs are 12 times each of them: 0, 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72.

chapters.title: Systems of Equations and Inequalities
chapters.bigQuestion: When two conditions must be true at the same time, how do you find the one answer that satisfies both?

story.title: The Bake Sale Budget
story.kicker: Cookies, brownies, one folding table and a $60 budget: the club needs an answer that fits every limit at once.
paragraphs: The robotics club at a Chicago high school runs a bake sale every October to pay for competition fees. Priya is treasurer this year, and she has last year's ledger in front of her. It says the club sold 120 items and took in $170, cookies at $1 and brownies at $2. Nobody wrote down how many of each. Priya wants to know, because brownies make more money but cost more to bake.

She writes what she knows as two sentences with letters. Let c be cookies and b be brownies. The count: c + b = 120. The money: 1c + 2b = 170. Two unknowns, two facts. She notices that if every item had been a cookie, the club would have made only $120. The extra $50 must have come from brownies, each of which brings in $1 more than a cookie. So there were 50 brownies and 120 − 50 = 70 cookies. Check: 70 + 50 = 120 items, and 70 + 100 = $170. Both facts are true at once.

This year is harder. The club's one folding table holds at most 150 items. Ingredients cost about $0.30 per cookie and $0.60 per brownie, and the budget is $60. Each cookie earns $0.70 profit and each brownie $1.50. Priya could bake 100 brownies and no cookies, but the faculty advisor insists on at least 40 cookies for the students who do not like chocolate. What mix makes the most money without breaking any limit?

Priya draws the limits on a grid, cookies across and brownies up. Each limit cuts the grid with a line, and the allowed region is the shape left in the middle. The best plan, it turns out, sits at a corner of that shape. Finding it takes the whole chapter: solving two equations together, graphing inequalities, and testing corners. By the end, Priya has a number, and the club has its fees.
story.think: Priya found 50 brownies and 70 cookies by reasoning 'the extra $50 must be brownies.' Try to explain why that reasoning works, using the two equations.

lessons.title: What a System Is
lessons.mainIdea: A system of equations is two or more equations about the same variables, and its solution makes every equation true at once.
reading: A single equation with two variables, like c + b = 120, has endless solutions: 0 and 120, 1 and 119, 60 and 60. It cannot tell you how many cookies were sold. A second fact, c + 2b = 170, also has endless solutions on its own. But only one pair fits both. Two equations that must hold at the same time form a *system of equations*, and the pair that makes both true is the *solution of the system*.

Test a candidate pair the same way you test a solution of one equation, but check every equation. Is (70, 50), meaning c = 70 and b = 50, the solution? First equation: 70 + 50 = 120, true. Second: 70 + 2(50) = 170, true. So yes. Is (60, 60) the solution? First: 60 + 60 = 120, true. Second: 60 + 120 = 180, not 170. It fails one equation, so it is not the solution. A pair must pass every test.

You can find a solution by *guess and check* in a table. Try b = 40: then c = 80 and the money is 80 + 80 = 160, too low. Try b = 50: c = 70 and the money is 70 + 100 = 170, right on. Each extra brownie adds $1, so the table climbs by 1 each row, and you can see exactly where it lands. The rest of this chapter replaces the table with faster methods, but the meaning stays the same: find the pair that satisfies both.

words.d: two or more equations that must be true at the same time for the same variables
the values that make every equation in the system true
trying values in a table and adjusting until every equation is satisfied

look.title: Trying Brownie Counts
look.cite: computed from c + b = 120 and c + 2b = money, with cookies $1 and brownies $2
look.prompt: Each row swaps 10 cookies for 10 brownies. Why does the money go up by exactly $10 each time?

check.q: Which pair (x, y) solves both x + y = 10 and x − y = 4?
check.why: 7 + 3 = 10 and 7 − 3 = 4, so both equations are true. (6, 4) gives 6 − 4 = 2, not 4.

check.q: Why is (60, 60) not the solution of c + b = 120 and c + 2b = 170?
choices: It fails the second equation, giving 180
It is not a whole-number pair
check.why: 60 + 60 = 120 works, but 60 + 2(60) = 180, not 170. A solution must satisfy every equation.

check.q: A system of two equations in two variables usually has…
check.why: Each equation alone has endless pairs, but usually only one pair fits both. Special cases with none or infinitely many come later.

lessons.title: Solving by Graphing
lessons.mainIdea: Graph both equations; the point where the lines cross is the solution, and reading it from the graph gives an estimate.
reading: Each equation in a system is a line, and every point on a line satisfies that equation. The solution of the system satisfies both, so it must lie on both lines. That is the *intersection*, the point where they cross. Take y = 2x + 1 and y = −x + 7. The first has *y-intercept* 1 and rises 2 for each step right. The second starts at 7 and falls 1 per step. Plot each line from its intercept and slope, and they cross at (2, 5).

Confirm by substituting: 2(2) + 1 = 5 and −2 + 7 = 5. Both equations give y = 5 at x = 2, so (2, 5) is the solution. When an equation is not in slope-intercept form, rewrite it first. For c + b = 120, solve for b: b = −c + 120. For c + 2b = 170, solve for b: 2b = −c + 170, so b = −0.5c + 85. The lines cross at c = 70, b = 50, the bake-sale answer.

Graphing shows the answer, but a hand-drawn graph is an *estimate*. If the lines cross at (2.4, 5.8), reading that from grid paper is hard. Use the graph to see roughly where the answer is and whether it makes sense, then use algebra to get it exactly. If two lines look parallel, expect no solution; if they lie on top of each other, every point is a solution.

words.d: the point where two graphs cross; it satisfies both equations
where a line crosses the vertical axis; the value of y when x is 0
an approximate answer read from a graph, to be checked with algebra

look.title: Two Lines on One Grid
look.text: Graph y = x + 1 and y = −2x + 7. The first starts at (0, 1) and climbs 1 per step. The second starts at (0, 7) and drops 2 per step. At x = 2 the first gives 3 and the second gives 3. They cross at (2, 3). Check: 2 + 1 = 3 and −4 + 7 = 3.
look.prompt: Graph y = 3x − 2 and y = x + 4. Where do they cross? Substitute your point into both equations to confirm.

check.q: Where do y = 2x + 1 and y = −x + 7 cross?
check.why: At x = 2, both give y = 5: 2(2) + 1 = 5 and −2 + 7 = 5. The other points fit at most one line.

check.q: Rewrite c + 2b = 170 in slope-intercept form for b.
check.why: Subtract c: 2b = −c + 170. Divide everything by 2: b = −0.5c + 85.

check.q: A hand-drawn graph shows two lines crossing near (3.2, 4.7). What should you do next?
choices: Solve with algebra to find the exact point
check.why: A graph gives an estimate. Algebra, such as substitution or elimination, gives the exact solution, which you then compare with the estimate.

lessons.title: Substitution
lessons.mainIdea: If one equation tells you what a variable equals, substitute that expression into the other equation and solve.
reading: Solve y = 2x + 1 and 3x + y = 16. The first equation already says what y is. Replace y in the second equation with 2x + 1: 3x + (2x + 1) = 16. Now there is one variable. Combine: 5x + 1 = 16. Subtract 1: 5x = 15. Divide: x = 3. Then find y from the first equation: y = 2(3) + 1 = 7. The solution is (3, 7). This method is *substitution*, and it works best when one equation is already solved for a variable or easily can be.

Check in both equations: 7 = 2(3) + 1 is true, and 3(3) + 7 = 16 is true. For the bake sale, c + b = 120 gives c = 120 − b. Substitute into c + 2b = 170: (120 − b) + 2b = 170, so 120 + b = 170 and b = 50. Then c = 120 − 50 = 70. The algebra is Priya's 'extra $50' reasoning written out.

Two errors are common. The first is substituting into the same equation you took the expression from, which gives a useless 0 = 0. Always substitute into the other one. The second is forgetting parentheses: in 4x − (x + 3) = 9, the minus must apply to the whole x + 3, giving 4x − x − 3 = 9, so 3x = 12 and x = 4. Writing 4x − x + 3 = 9 by mistake gives x = 2, and the check fails.

words.d: replacing a variable with an expression it equals, so an equation has only one variable
a combination of numbers and variables, like 2x + 1, that stands for a value
put the solution back into every original equation to confirm both are true

look.title: Substitute, Then Back-Substitute
look.text: Solve x = y + 4 and 2x + 3y = 23. Replace x in the second equation: 2(y + 4) + 3y = 23. Distribute: 2y + 8 + 3y = 23. Combine: 5y + 8 = 23, so 5y = 15 and y = 3. Then x = 3 + 4 = 7. Check: 2(7) + 3(3) = 14 + 9 = 23.
look.prompt: Solve y = 3x − 5 and 2x + y = 10 by substitution, and check your pair in both equations.

check.q: Solve y = 2x + 1 and 3x + y = 16.
Solve y = 3x − 5 and 2x + y = 10.
Solving 4x − (x + 3) = 9, a student writes 4x − x + 3 = 9. What went wrong?
choices: The x terms cannot be combined
The minus sign was not distributed to the 3
The 9 should have been moved first
check.why: Subtracting the whole expression gives 4x − x − 3 = 9, so 3x = 12 and x = 4. The student's version gives x = 2, which fails the check.

lessons.title: Elimination by Adding
lessons.mainIdea: Adding two equations together is legal because you add equal amounts to both sides, and it can make one variable disappear.
reading: Take x + y = 10 and x − y = 4. The y terms are opposites: +y and −y. Add the two equations, left side to left side and right side to right side: (x + y) + (x − y) = 10 + 4, which is 2x = 14, so x = 7. The y vanished. Substitute back: 7 + y = 10, so y = 3. Solution (7, 3). Check the second: 7 − 3 = 4. This method is *elimination*.

Why is adding equations allowed? The second equation says x − y and 4 are the same number. Adding the same number to both sides of the first equation keeps it true; you just wrote that number two different ways. This is the addition property of equality from the first chapter, applied to a whole equation. If the matching terms are equal rather than opposite, subtract instead. From 3x + 2y = 19 and x + 2y = 9, subtracting gives 2x = 10, so x = 5 and then 2y = 4, y = 2.

Sign errors are the usual trouble. When subtracting, subtract every term of the second equation, including its right side. And after finding one variable, find the other by substituting into an original equation, not into the combined one. Finally, check the pair in both originals: 3(5) + 2(2) = 19 and 5 + 4 = 9. Both true, so (5, 2) is right.

words.d: adding or subtracting equations so that one variable cancels out
terms like +2y and −2y that add to zero
adding the same amount to both sides of an equation keeps it true

look.title: Opposites Cancel
look.text: Solve 2x + 3y = 13 and 4x − 3y = 5. The 3y terms are opposites, so add: 6x = 18 and x = 3. Substitute into the first: 6 + 3y = 13, so 3y = 7 and y = 7/3. Check the second: 4(3) − 3(7/3) = 12 − 7 = 5. Not every answer is a whole number, and that is fine.
look.prompt: Solve 5x + 2y = 16 and 3x − 2y = 8 by adding. Check your answer in both equations.

check.q: Solve x + y = 10 and x − y = 4 by elimination.
check.why: Adding gives 2x = 14, so x = 7, then y = 3. Check: 7 − 3 = 4.

check.q: Solve 5x + 2y = 16 and 3x − 2y = 8.
check.why: Adding gives 8x = 24, so x = 3. Then 15 + 2y = 16, so y = 1/2. Check: 9 − 1 = 8.

check.q: Why can you add two equations of a system together?
choices: Because both sides of each equation are equal, so you add equal amounts to both sides
Because the variables are the same letters
Because adding always removes a variable
Because the equations are both lines
check.why: The second equation says its two sides are the same number, so adding them to the two sides of the first equation keeps it balanced.

lessons.title: Elimination with Multiplying
lessons.mainIdea: Multiply one or both equations by a number first so that a pair of terms becomes opposites, then add.
reading: Solve 2x + 3y = 12 and 4x − y = 10. Nothing cancels yet: adding gives 6x + 2y = 22, still two variables. But multiplying the whole second equation by 3 gives 12x − 3y = 30, and now the y terms are opposites of the 3y in the first equation. Multiplying both sides by 3 is the multiplication property of equality, so the new equation is *equivalent* to the old one. Add: (2x + 3y) + (12x − 3y) = 12 + 30, so 14x = 42 and x = 3.

Substitute into an original: 4(3) − y = 10, so y = 2. Check the first: 2(3) + 3(2) = 6 + 6 = 12. Solution (3, 2). Sometimes both equations need multiplying. For 3x + 2y = 7 and 2x + 5y = 12, multiply the first by 2 and the second by −3 to get 6x + 4y = 14 and −6x − 15y = −36. Add: −11y = −22, so y = 2. Then 3x + 4 = 7 gives x = 1. Check the second: 2 + 10 = 12.

Choose the *multiplier* by finding a common multiple of the two coefficients you want to cancel, and give one of them a negative sign. The classic slip is multiplying only the left side of an equation. Every term, including the constant on the right, gets multiplied. Another is forgetting the sign change, which makes the terms add instead of cancel. When the combined equation still has two variables, look back for one of those two mistakes.

words.d: the number you multiply a whole equation by to set up a cancellation
an equation with the same solutions as another; multiplying both sides by a nonzero number keeps them equivalent
a number that two coefficients both divide into, like 6 for 2 and 3

look.title: Set Up the Cancel
look.text: Solve 3x + 4y = 26 and 5x − 2y = 13. Multiply the second by 2: 10x − 4y = 26. Add to the first: 13x = 52, so x = 4. Then 12 + 4y = 26, so 4y = 14 and y = 3.5. Check the second: 5(4) − 2(3.5) = 20 − 7 = 13.
look.prompt: Solve 2x + 5y = 1 and 3x + 2y = 7 by multiplying both equations. Which multipliers did you pick and why?

check.q: Solve 2x + 3y = 12 and 4x − y = 10.
check.why: Multiply the second by 3 and add: 14x = 42, so x = 3. Then 12 − y = 10 gives y = 2. Check: 6 + 6 = 12.

check.q: To eliminate y from 3x + 2y = 7 and 2x + 5y = 12, which multipliers work?
choices: Multiply the first by 2 and the second by 3
Multiply the first by 5 and the second by 2, then add
Multiply the first by 5 and the second by −2
check.why: 10y and −10y cancel: 15x + 10y = 35 and −4x − 10y = −24 add to 11x = 11, so x = 1 and y = 2.

check.q: A student multiplies 4x − y = 10 by 3 and writes 12x − 3y = 10. What is wrong?
choices: The right side must also be multiplied, giving 30
check.why: Multiplying both sides by 3 means 10 becomes 30. Leaving the 10 makes the new equation not equivalent to the original.

lessons.title: No Solution or Infinitely Many
lessons.mainIdea: Parallel lines give a system no solution, and two forms of the same line give infinitely many.
reading: Consider y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3. Both have slope 2, so they are *parallel lines* that never cross. Try substitution anyway: 2x + 1 = 2x − 3. Subtract 2x from both sides: 1 = −3. That is false no matter what x is. When the variables vanish and leave a false statement, the system has *no solution*. No pair of numbers can be on both lines.

Now consider 2x + 4y = 8 and x + 2y = 4. Multiply the second by 2: 2x + 4y = 8, identical to the first. They are the same line written two ways, so every point on the line works: (4, 0), (0, 2), (2, 1) and infinitely many more. Elimination shows it: subtract the doubled second equation from the first and you get 0 = 0, a statement that is always true. That signals *infinitely many solutions*.

So there are three outcomes. If solving gives a specific x, the lines cross once and there is one solution. If the variables cancel and leave something false like 1 = −3, there is no solution. If they cancel and leave something true like 0 = 0, there are infinitely many. In a story, no solution might mean two plans never cost the same, and infinitely many might mean two 'different' facts were really the same fact.
